• Prometheus: name (unique), group, severity, PromQL expression, delay before alert (5m), summary, description (variables {{ $value }}, {{ $labels.job }}), group evaluation interval (that of the group's first rule), active.
  • Grafana: title, identifier (UID, derived from the title if empty), folder, group, interval, data source (prometheus: PromQL; other, e.g. postgresql: raw SQL), query, window (seconds), delay, severity, summary, description, "no data" and "execution error" states, active.
  • Durations: 30s, 5m, 1h30m (units ms s m h d w y).

docs.title: Files and reload
docs.text:
Variable Role PROMETHEUS_RULES_PATH, PROMETHEUS_URL rules.yml file; POST /-/reload GRAFANA_ALERTING_PATH, GRAFANA_URL, GRAFANA_USER, GRAFANA_PASSWORD rules.yaml file; POST /api/admin/provisioning/alerting/reload

The file is written atomically. If the reload fails (service stopped, refusal), the file stays written and the page says so; the service will read it at its next start. With no path configured, the service is "not configured" (nothing written). dominet sync-rules does the same on the command line; writing also happens when the server starts.

docs.title: "No data" state of the shipped rules
docs.text: The four shipped Grafana rules have their "no data" state set to OK. A query such as up == 0 or "5xx rate" returns nothing while everything is fine: with NoData (the former system's setting), Grafana sent an anomaly alert at every evaluation, observed during the production installation (R8). If you create your own rules of this kind, choose OK. An installation already made with the old setting is fixed in /admin/grafana-rules (existing rules are never modified by dominet seed).

docs.title: Verification
docs.text: The files produced are compared with frozen reference values. See ADR 0052.

docs.title: Publishers (weather, SolarMax) and context
docs.text: Integrations that read an external source and publish to MQTT (R3 lot 6). Decisions: ADR 0030. The messages become devices through the MQTT sources (meteo/#, solarmax/#).

docs.title: Running
docs.text:
• dominet serve runs the publishers role when MQTT_HOST is set; --only publishers for a separate process (MQTT client …-publishers). Tasks are supervised (restarted after a panic).
  • Weather: enabled stations of /admin/weather-stations (Open-Meteo, no key). Without an enabled station no request is made (the database is re-read every 30 s). Creating or editing a station triggers an immediate reading; then one reading every refresh_minutes (the shortest among stations). Published on meteo/<suffix>. dominet seed-weather --lat 43.3 --lon 5.4 creates the "Météo" source, the meteo_locale device (tracked keys: temperature, humidity, precipitation, wind) and the station.
  • SolarMax: only if SOLARMAX_HOST is set — it has no default value (the production inverter is never contacted by mistake). One cycle every SOLARMAX_INTERVAL_SECS s (10): detection, values (pac, eac, pdc, edc, qdy, qt0, tmpr, status), status and alarms; an inverter alarm is not published. Published on SOLARMAX_TOPIC (default solarmax/0x6f0930a64c8b8803/prod, the default topic).
Variable Default Role OPEN_METEO_URL https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast API address (a simulated API for tests) SOLARMAX_HOST — inverter to query; without it, no SolarMax publisher SOLARMAX_PORT, SOLARMAX_INVERTER_ID 12345, 1 TCP port, inverter number (1 to 99) SOLARMAX_TOPIC solarmax/0x6f0930a64c8b8803/prod publication topic SOLARMAX_INTERVAL_SECS 10 interval between two readings (1 to 3600)

docs.title: Diagnostics
docs.text:
• dominet publish weather [--print-only]: one reading per enabled station; prints the JSON and publishes it (unless --print-only).
  • dominet publish solarmax [--print-only]: one cycle; refuses to run without SOLARMAX_HOST. The inverter accepts a single TCP client at a time: run while the publishers role is active (the normal case in production), the command fails ("did not answer in time") although the service publishes normally. To check the reading without stopping the service, look at the SolarMax device in the interface or at the Logs page (/admin/logs, text solarmax); for a manual reading, stop the stack first (make prod-down), then start it again (make prod-up).
  • dominet dump-context [--output context.yaml]: YAML snapshot of active devices (type, state schema inferred from current values, numeric keys, command topic, location), active scenes, automations and device alert rules (R7 lot 8), Grafana rules and reference schemas.

docs.title: Simulators (tests, demonstration)
docs.text: tools/sim-open-meteo.py PORT (weather API, fixed reading, /__count counter) and tools/sim-solarmax.py PORT (inverter, full protocol) only listen on 127.0.0.1. Rust tests have their own simulated inverter (dominet_integrations::solarmax::sim). tools/e2e.sh starts them and points the server at them.

docs.title: Checking with reference values
docs.text:
• tests/fixtures/solarmax/vectors.json holds frozen reference vectors (requests, answers, scaling, rounding), produced without network: the constructor, which connects to the inverter, is never called. The Rust tests require the same results.
  • tests/fixtures/context/schemas.json holds the reference state schemas (_state_schema, _numeric_keys).

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: cargo test -p dominet-integrations (protocol, client against the simulated inverter, weather against the simulated API, supervision), -p dominet-server --test publishers (simulated API and inverter → publisher → dev Mosquitto → source → device), --test context, -p dominet --test ui (stations), E2E weather.

docs.title: Quick install
docs.text: The guided installer checks your machine, asks four questions and deploys the application. It takes a few minutes of your time; the first start may take longer while images are built or downloaded.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A machine that stays on at home: a mini PC, a small server or a Raspberry Pi 5 (see Supported machines and Measurements for what each holds). Linux, with Docker and the Docker Compose plugin (version 2.24 or newer), plus git, make, openssl and curl.
  • At least 2 GB of memory (4 GB or more recommended) and 10 GB of free disk space (video recordings need much more).
  • Your user must be able to run docker (member of the docker group).

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/deunix-educ/domia-automation.git
cd domia-automation
./install.sh

The installer goes through four steps and stops with a clear message if something blocks:

  1. Checks the machine: system, Docker and Compose versions, memory, disk space, free ports (80, 443, 1883), architecture.
  2. Asks a few questions: the address the devices will use (default <machine name>.local), the administrator account name and password (hidden, at least 10 characters), an e-mail address for alerts (optional). It detects a Zigbee dongle and hardware video decoding by itself.
  3. Writes the configuration (.env, readable by you only): all passwords and keys are generated for you and never displayed.
  4. Deploys: certificates, build or download, start, administrator account, first data, final check.

docs.title: Try it first
docs.text:
./install.sh --dry-run

runs the checks and the questions and changes nothing. ./install.sh --help lists the options (--yes for unattended use, --domain, --admin, --email, --no-zigbee, --reuse, --lang fr|en).

docs.title: After the installation
docs.text:
1. Open https://<address> and sign in with the administrator account.
  2. On each phone and computer, install the certificate once by opening http://<address>/dominet-ca.crt (the application uses a certificate signed by your own authority; the page explains why browsers ask).
  3. Copy DOMINET_MASTER_KEY from .env to a safe place away from the machine. Without it, a restored backup loses the encrypted secrets (camera passwords).
  4. Add your devices and cameras; the rest of this documentation describes each page.

docs.title: Images
docs.text: The installer first tries a ready-made image (amd64 and arm64) from the project's registry, which saves 15 to 40 minutes of compilation; if it is not available (offline, before publication, a fork) it builds the image on the machine. DOMINET_PULL=0 in .env forces the build; DOMINET_IMAGE_VERSION pins a release. See ADR 0062.

docs.title: If something goes wrong
docs.text:
• The installer names the blocking point and how to fix it (for example "the port 443 is already used": stop what uses it).
  • It never overwrites an existing .env. To redo a failed deployment with the same configuration: ./install.sh --reuse.
  • To follow the application's messages: make prod-logs S=dominet N=100.
  • The diagnosis, read-only, which says what to fix: make prod-doctor (see Troubleshooting).
  • Before installing: make preflight.

For the manual procedure, every option and the update routine, see Production deployment.

docs.title: Rebuilding from scratch
docs.text: The order in which to build the application, what to write first, which traps to read before each step and how to know a step is done. It assumes you have read Pitfalls and lessons, Measurements and Decisions by theme; each step below points at the parts that matter.

docs.title: Principles
docs.text:
• One phase at a time, then stop and check. A phase ends with its definition of done and a demonstration; the next one does not start before that is accepted.
  • Write the reference data first. Recorded device sessions, expected alert and schedule results, protocol vectors and camera answers are cheap to produce early and expensive to guess later. Tests that compare against such files caught most of the subtle defects (see the pitfalls page, domain logic).
  • A throw-away spike before any architecture for every risky technique, with a written verdict (go, go with reservations, no-go with the alternative) and an ADR.
  • Run the whole gate often. make ci (format, clippy with warnings as errors, tests, WASM build, cargo deny, cargo audit, SQL metadata check) before every commit; make ci-full (adds the Docker image and the browser tests on it) before a milestone or when the Dockerfile or a native dependency changes.
  • Rehearse on the real machine as early as the phase allows: decoding, certificates, mail and disk problems appear nowhere else.
  • No secret, real address or personal image in the repository, logs, dumps or fixtures.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Rust 1.99.1 (edition 2024, pinned in rust-toolchain.toml) with the wasm32-unknown-unknown target; cargo-leptos 0.3.11, sqlx-cli, cargo-deny, cargo-audit; Docker with Compose; ffmpeg with the VAAPI driver on the target; a browser driver for the end-to-end tests. Build with a baseline CPU level (x86-64-v2), never target-cpu=native. Keep .cargo/config.toml as it is: it makes the server and the WASM compile alike.

docs.title: Workspace
docs.text:
One Cargo workspace, one binary with roles. Crates by responsibility, from the inside out:

Crate Role dominet-proto data types shared by the server and the browser dominet-domain pure rules and validation, no I/O dominet-store PostgreSQL repositories and migrations dominet-mqtt the supervised MQTT client dominet-automation automation engine, scheduler, script host, alerts, energy balance dominet-notify e-mail and SMS channels dominet-integrations weather and solar-inverter publishers dominet-surveillance cameras, ONVIF, MediaMTX client, motion, detection, frames dominet-server HTTP and WebSocket server, services shared by the interface and MCP dominet-web the Leptos interface dominet-mcp the MCP server dominet-agent the local assistant loop dominet the binary: sub-commands and roles (web, mqtt, scheduler, video, publishers, discovery)

docs.title: Build order
docs.text:
# Phase What to build Read first Done when 0 Spikes Eight throw-away experiments: server-rendered interface with WebSocket and translations; raw time-series store at one million records; WHEP live view in WASM; H.264 decoding cost; object detection latency; ONVIF against real cameras; sandboxed scripts; MQTT client under load Measurements §1; decisions on video each spike has a verdict and an ADR 1 Foundations Typed configuration from environment variables, tracing, health endpoints, migrations, login with server-side sessions, hashed passwords and lockout, typed settings with masked secrets, seed data, the interface shell (layout, dark theme, navigation, language switch, generic CRUD), administration pages Pitfalls §1 to §4 login works, CRUD pages work, authentication tests pass (including lockout and races), the image builds and starts 2 Real time and dashboard WebSocket hub with typed topics that keep the last state; dashboard and widgets with drag and drop and persistence; system statistics Pitfalls §2; decision on the frozen-render guard a message updates a widget without reload; browser tests green 3 MQTT and devices Supervised listener, Zigbee2MQTT ingestion, dynamic MQTT sources, history in the database and the raw store, device commands, pairing, groups and labels, weather and solar publishers, context dump Pitfalls §5 a recorded session replays into the same devices, states and history rows; broker outage tested; sustained throughput validated 4 Automations, scenes, alerts, energy Engine (message, schedule, solar and device-state triggers; publish, script, notification and scene actions), in-process scheduler, script host with limits, scenes, alert rules with lifecycle and acknowledgement, daily energy balance Pitfalls §5, §7; decisions on automation real scenarios run identically; cooldowns hold; a hostile script is stopped without harming the process 5 Notifications, messaging, phone relay SMTP and SMS channels, internal messaging, the Android relay with its frozen WebSocket contract Decisions on messaging the unmodified phone app connects, sends and receives, acknowledges; contract tests pass 6 Surveillance Cameras and MediaMTX path sync, live view, ONVIF discovery and PTZ, night-mode backends, recording and replay, snapshots, motion detection, object detection, the frame-source abstraction Pitfalls §6; Measurements §2 live under 1 s on the LAN; one hour of continuous recording with no lost segment; detection matches reference; CPU and memory measured on the target 7 Observability and operations Metrics endpoint, Prometheus and Grafana rules and dashboards, backups with tested restore, Compose base and overlays, reverse proxy with TLS, Makefile, documentation site, deployment guide Pitfalls §8, §9 a blank machine installs in three commands; a restore is validated 8 Acceptance and production Parity checklist run on the real machine, load tests, blank-install rehearsal, switch-over procedure, 48-hour watch Measurements §3, §4; Pitfalls §9 checklist validated by the owner, installation reproducible, rollback rehearsed 9 MCP server Server built into the binary, scoped hashed tokens, audit written before execution, read then control then configuration then administration tools, a shared configuration service used by the interface too Pitfalls §11; decisions on MCP every tool has a dry run where it changes something; scope matrix tested 10 Local assistant Agent loop calling the MCP tools in memory and a self-hosted model; action cards confirmed by the user; snapshot, undo and audit Pitfalls §11; Measurements §5 evaluation set passes its threshold with no wrong card 11 Platform alerts Read-only view of Prometheus and Grafana alerts in the alerts page and the badge Pitfalls §8 both sources, unreachable-source state and the badge covered by tests

Dependencies: 0 to 1 to 2 to 3 to 4 to 7 to 8 is the critical path. 5 and 6 can run beside 3 and 4 once 2 is done. 9 to 11 come after 8.

docs.title: Definition of done for every phase
docs.text:
• Every feature is delivered and reachable from the interface.
  • Unit, integration and contract tests pass; critical paths are covered.
  • Format, lints as errors, cargo deny and cargo audit are clean.
  • The Docker image builds and answers its health check.
  • Documentation (both languages) and ADRs are updated.
  • No sensitive data in logs, dumps or fixtures.
  • A step-by-step demonstration is written, then you wait for validation.

docs.title: Risks to keep in view
docs.text: Risk Mitigation No mature pure-Rust H.264 decoder ffmpeg subprocess behind a frame-source trait; revisit only with measurements The raw store is not a time-series database aggregates in PostgreSQL, raw history in the store Replacing a generated admin site (about thirty CRUD screens) one generic CRUD component from phase 1 WebRTC and drag and drop in WASM minimal, isolated JavaScript interop; spike first ONVIF variety across camera families minimal client, real-camera tests, recorded SOAP fixtures ARM images build natively on an ARM machine, not by emulation Scope for one developer short phases, parity per module, optional phases kept optional

docs.title: Releasing and going public
docs.text: Maintainer's runbook. Nothing here is automatic: there is no CI service (ADR 0015), the gate is make ci run locally. The repository stays private until the owner gives an explicit go.

docs.title: 1. Before the first publication
docs.text:
1. Decide the history. The public repository can start from a single commit ("Initial public release") so the working history does not appear. Squash on a copy and compare trees: bash tree=$(git rev-parse 'HEAD^{tree}') GIT_AUTHOR_NAME=... GIT_AUTHOR_EMAIL=... GIT_COMMITTER_NAME=... GIT_COMMITTER_EMAIL=... \ git branch -f public "$(git commit-tree "$tree" -m 'Initial public release')" git diff HEAD public | wc -l # must print 0
  2. Decide the identity shown on commits (name and e-mail). Check with git log --format='%an <%ae>' | sort -u; rewrite the author on the squashed commit if it must not be public (git commit --amend --reset-author after setting user.name and user.email).
  3. Scan: tools/public-scan.sh --files. The remaining findings must all be explained: private addresses are examples and test data (RFC 1918 ranges), dominet.local is the product's default name, "secrets" are test passwords and variable names. Anything else is fixed first.
  4. Gate: make ci-full green, make docs clean, make check-migrate green (stop the dev stack first), tools/check-installer.sh green.
  5. Dependencies: cargo audit and cargo deny check have no unexplained entry; re-read Licences and update the "verified" dates.
  6. Version: set version in Cargo.toml (workspace) to the release number, refresh Cargo.lock (cargo update -w), move the Unreleased section of CHANGELOG.md under the new number and date.

docs.title: 2. Create the repository (private first)
docs.text:
On GitHub: a private repository domia-automation, no template files (they are in the tree). Push the squashed branch as main (the working branch stays local):

git remote add origin git@github.com:<owner>/domia-automation.git
git push -u origin public:main   # the pre-push hook reruns make ci on a clean copy (about 15 minutes)

Settings to set while it is still private: enable Private vulnerability reporting (Security, Code security), the issue templates are already in .github/, add topics (home-automation, rust, mqtt, zigbee2mqtt, self-hosted), a short description, disable Wiki and Projects if unused, protect main (no force-push).

docs.title: 3. Publish the artefacts
docs.text:
git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "1.0.0" && git push origin v1.0.0
PLATFORMS=linux/amd64 VERSION=1.0.0 tools/publish-image.sh   # first release: amd64 only; log in first (docker login ghcr.io)
make docs-deploy                              # builds the site and pushes the gh-pages branch

Create the GitHub release from the tag with the CHANGELOG.md section. Check on a clean machine: git clone, ./install.sh --dry-run, then a real installation that pulls the image.

The first release is amd64 only: the arm64 image is published (drop PLATFORMS) after it has been built and started on a real arm64 machine at least once (ADR 0063). Until then arm64 machines build the image locally.

docs.title: 4. Go public
docs.text:
Only after an explicit "go" from the owner: Settings, General, Danger Zone, Change visibility. Then enable GitHub Pages from the gh-pages branch, make the package public on GHCR, and re-run the clean-machine installation from the public URLs.

Going back is not a real option: assume everything pushed is copied within minutes. If a secret slips out, rotate it first, then rewrite the history.

docs.title: 5. Later releases
docs.text: make ci-full, update CHANGELOG.md, bump the version, tag, tools/publish-image.sh, make docs-deploy. Migrations never edit an applied file; a rewording needs an entry like the one in crates/dominet-store/src/lib.rs.

docs.title: Scenes
docs.text:
Pages, activation and administration of scenes (R4 lot 2). Decisions: ADR 0031 (schema and domain), R4 plan (D12: permissions).

A scene is a set of commands applied together to several devices ("Evening closing": six shutters and lamps). It has a (unique) name, an icon (emoji or name), a description, a location, an active / inactive state and an ordered list of commands (device + JSON object, e.g. {"state":"CLOSE"}).

docs.title: For every account
docs.text:
• /automation/scenes (the "Scenes" link on the devices page): the active scenes, one card each with its commands in order and an Activate button. Feedback appears next to the button: ✓ Scene activated, or ✗ followed by each device whose command did not go out and why (not found or inactive, refused, source unavailable).
  • Scene widget on the dashboard: the name, the description and the same button. A deleted or disabled scene is announced in the widget.
  • Activation = publish each command on <prefix>/<device name>/set, in order, QoS 1. A failing command does not stop the following ones: failures are reported at the end. Any signed-in account may activate(the family runs "Evening closing").

docs.title: For administrators
docs.text:
• /admin/scenes: filterable list, add, edit, delete with confirmation. The command editor is a list of rows (device chosen from a dropdown, JSON command) with ↑ ↓ to reorder, × to remove and "Add a command". Errors are reported on the field: empty or taken name, command that is not an accepted JSON object (non-empty object, bounded depth and size), unknown device, more than 100 commands.
  • Widgets (/admin/widgets): a widget's scene is picked from a dropdown (no number to know).
  • Deleting a scene deletes its commands; widgets that pointed at it lose their scene, and automations that activated it fail (written to the automation log).

docs.title: Notable behaviors
docs.text:
• A scene's name is unique (the script API activates a scene by name).
  • A command to an inactive device is reported as failed (not found or inactive) instead of being published.
  • A disabled scene can no longer be activated (answer 404).

docs.title: For developers
docs.text:
• dominet_server::scenes::{activate, activate_by_id, activate_by_name}: the automation engine (lot 3) and the script API (lot 5) go through them. They rely on control::send_command (immediate refusal without a broker link).
  • Server functions: scenes/list, scenes/activate (any signed-in account), scenes-admin/{list,save,delete} (administrators).
  • The form uses the generic CRUD field type FieldKind::Pairs (list of choice + text pairs, form value = JSON [["12","{…}"],…], choices supplied by the Choices context under the field name).

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: cargo test -p dominet --test ui scene (permissions, field-by-field validation, page), -p dominet-server --test scenes (publication in order on the dev broker, a failure does not stop the rest, the three production scenes: 6 / 4 / 4 commands on the right topics), -p dominet-store --test automation (storage); E2E scenes (full run in Firefox).

docs.title: Rhai scripts
docs.text:
Automation scripts (script action) and handler code of MQTT sources (R4 lot 5). Decisions: ADR 0006 (spike), ADR 0034 (implementation).

Scripts are written in Rhai, an embedded language close to Rust/JavaScript. Python code does not port as is: it is refused when saving with a clear message (def, import, trailing colons, context.…).

docs.title: What a script sees
docs.text: Name Content topic topic of the message or state that triggered the script (empty for a scheduled or solar trigger) payload the message: object (payload.temperature) or text; a missing key is () (never an error) device the device concerned or (); fields below Device field Content name, id, type name, number and type (light, cover, sensor…) state last known state (device.state.position) available true if the device is reachable topic topic of its state (zigbee2mqtt/Salon); append "/set" to command it age_secs age of its last message in seconds (decimal number, frozen when the script starts), or () if it never spoke Function Effect publish(topic, message) publishes on the broker (QoS 1, not retained). Text is published as is; a map (#{ state: "ON" }) or a number as JSON. No wildcard in the topic, 256 characters at most. Alias: mqtt_publish scene(name) activates the scene of that name get_device(name) reads a device (same fields as device), or () if it does not exist log_value(key, value) records a value of the device concerned, tracked or not (no effect without a device) print(text), log(text) line of the execution log (50 lines, 500 characters)

docs.title: Sandbox rules
docs.text:
• No direct effect. publish, scene and log_value are set aside and applied in order after the script ends, and only if it ends without error (all or nothing). At most 100 effects per run.
  • Limits: 200,000 operations, 250 ms, 24 call levels, expressions 48 levels deep, 16 KB strings, 2,000-element arrays, 500-key maps. No eval, no import. An infinite loop, endless recursion or giant allocation is interrupted without affecting the process: the server keeps answering, the error is written to the automation's log.
  • Each run happens in a separate thread (a panic there is an error).
  • A script automation counts toward the guard of 30 firings per minute.

docs.title: Where to write a script
docs.text:
• Automation: /admin/automations, "Script" action. MQTT source: /admin/mqtt-sources, "Handler code" field (variables topic and payload, same functions; no execution log, the result goes to the server log; a failing code is muted for 10 s).
  • Syntax is checked when saving: the parser's error (line, column) shows under the field.
  • Dry run (button under the code area, administrators): runs the script with a sample topic and message against the real device states and shows what it would have done — without publishing, activating or recording anything.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
// Turn the living room on above 25 degrees, and keep the value
if payload.temperature > 25.0 {
    publish("zigbee2mqtt/Salon/set", #{ state: "ON" });
}
log_value("temperature_bureau", payload.temperature);

// Open the blind only if the door is closed
let porte = get_device("Porte");
if porte != () && porte.state.contact == true {
    publish("zigbee2mqtt/Volet-salon/set", #{ state: "OPEN" });
}

docs.title: The two scripts of the SB-est shutter
docs.text:
The two Volet-SB-est scripts are written in Rhai (crates/dominet-domain/data/volet-sb-est-*.rhai, device_state trigger on the switch's action, single_left and single_right). The left button opens, the right one closes, and a press during travel stops the shutter.

The real relay (Relais-SB-est) has neither a moving key nor a STOP state: its state derives from the position. It publishes about one message per second while moving, then goes silent; the script therefore treats it as moving if its last message is less than 2 seconds old (age_secs):

let volet = get_device("Relais-SB-est");
if volet == () {
    throw "appareil Relais-SB-est introuvable";
}
let commande = volet.topic + "/set";
if volet.age_secs != () && volet.age_secs < 2.0 {
    publish(commande, #{ state: "STOP" });
} else {
    publish(commande, #{ state: "OPEN" });   // "CLOSE" for the right button
}

To use them: create two "device state" automations on the switch (key action, value single_left then single_right), "Script" action, and paste this code (adapting the relay's name). They replace the two simple "open" and "close" automations.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: cargo test -p dominet-automation --lib script (API, effects in order, all or nothing, hostile scripts: loops, recursion, giant strings / arrays / maps, pad, eval, nesting, endless effects; time limit alone; another language refused), --test engine (scripts in the engine, production plugins, muted source code), -p dominet --test ui script (dry run, syntax, permissions), -p dominet-server --test automations (end to end on the dev broker); E2E automations (editor, dry run, execution, infinite loop while the server keeps answering).

docs.title: Security
docs.text: DomiNet is designed for a home network you control. This page says what is protected, what is deliberately open on the LAN, and what must never be exposed to the Internet. To report a problem, see SECURITY.md at the root of the repository.

docs.title: What is exposed by the production stack
docs.text: Port Service Who can reach it Protection 443 (80 redirects) nginx, the application, Grafana under /grafana/ the LAN TLS; the application requires a login; the only unauthenticated routes are the login page, the health probe and the certificate download (/dominet-ca.crt, also on HTTP so a new device can get it) 1883 MQTT (Mosquitto) the LAN password required for every client, rights per account on a topic; no anonymous listener 8554 RTSP (MediaMTX) the LAN no password: anyone on the LAN can watch the camera streams (see below) 8189 (udp, tcp) WebRTC (MediaMTX) the LAN no password, same reason 8080 Zigbee2MQTT interface (only with a dongle) the LAN access token (ZIGBEE_AUTH_TOKEN) 51820 (udp) and the wg-easy interface optional VPN profile the Internet if you forward it WireGuard keys; the web interface is protected by WG_ADMIN_HASH 5432 PostgreSQL this machine only (127.0.0.1) password 8181 Adminer (optional profile) this machine only (127.0.0.1) database password 9997, 9998, 9100, Prometheus, Grafana's own port internal APIs and metrics the Docker network only not published

docs.title: What has no password, on purpose
docs.text: Viewing a camera over RTSP or WebRTC needs no password: the browser, the phone applications and VLC read the streams directly. Publishing to MediaMTX and its API are restricted to the Docker network and this machine. The consequence is simple: anyone connected to your home network can watch your cameras. Keep guests on a separate network or Wi-Fi, and never forward ports 8554 or 8189 on your router. Per-viewer credentials are on the improvement list (To improve).

docs.title: What is protected
docs.text:
• Accounts: argon2id hashes, server-side sessions (opaque cookie, idle and absolute expiry), CSRF protection, lock-out after repeated failures (per account and address, per account, per address), password changes close every session. Passwords: 10 to 128 characters, not only digits, not the user name.
  • Secrets stored in the database (camera passwords, SMS keys) are encrypted with DOMINET_MASTER_KEY (AES-256-GCM). Keep a copy of that key away from the machine: it is not in the backups.
  • Generated secrets: make prod-init generates every password and token; there is no default password anywhere, and make prod-guard refuses an empty or placeholder value. .env is created with mode 600 and is never committed (only the .env.example.* templates are).
  • Containers: the application runs as a non-root user, the images are pinned to a version, and the database has no network access from outside the machine.
  • MCP server (optional, off by default): access tokens are hashed, scoped, revocable and must expire; every call is audited (MCP audit).
  • Scripts of automations run in a sandbox with an operation limit.
  • Dependencies: cargo deny (licences, sources) and cargo audit (vulnerabilities) run in make ci. The advisories that are accepted, with the reason, are listed in deny.toml.

docs.title: Checklist for a safe installation
docs.text:
1. Install on a machine reachable only from your LAN; do not forward ports 80, 443, 1883, 8554, 8189 or 8080 on the router.
  2. For remote access use the WireGuard profile (one UDP port) or your own VPN, with a strong WG_ADMIN_HASH.
  3. Keep .env and the migration archives private (they hold keys); keep DOMINET_MASTER_KEY in a password manager.
  4. Install the certificate authority on your devices (/dominet-ca.crt) rather than clicking through browser warnings.
  5. Update with make prod-update regularly; read the release notes (CHANGELOG.md).
  6. Run make prod-doctor after any change.

docs.title: Application settings
docs.text:
Seventeen settings editable without a restart, stored in the database (app_setting), typed (str, int, float, bool) and grouped by category. A setting missing from the database takes its default value: the application works before dominet seed.

Category Key Type Default Notifications EMAIL_RECIPIENT str dominet@localhost Notifications DEFAULT_FROM_EMAIL str dominet@localhost Notifications SMS_FREE_USER str (empty) Notifications SMS_FREE_KEY str, secret (empty) Alerts PROMETHEUS_ALERT_COOLDOWN int (s) 3600 Alerts MOTION_ALERT_COOLDOWN int (s) 600 Surveillance MOTION_THRESHOLD float (0.0–1.0) 0.01 Surveillance RECORDINGS_SEGMENT_DURATION int (s) 60 Interface GRAFANA_PUBLIC_URL str http://localhost:3000 — origin allowed for the dashboard's Grafana iframes (CSP frame-src, ADR 0022) Interface PROMETHEUS_PUBLIC_URL str http://localhost:9090 Interface MEDIAMTX_WEBRTC_DOMAIN str localhost:8889 Interface MEDIAMTX_WEBRTC_SCHEME str http MQTT Z2M_BASE_TOPIC str zigbee2mqtt Assistant AGENT_ENABLED bool false — enables the Assistant page (R12) Assistant AGENT_LLM_URL str (empty) — address of llama-server, ex. http://192.168.1.20:8081 Assistant AGENT_MODEL str Qwen3-8B-Q4_K_M — everyday requests Assistant AGENT_MODEL_ADMIN str (empty) — model for configuration requests; empty = same as AGENT_MODEL

Values: decimals use a dot (0.01), booleans true/false/oui/non/1/0. A value incompatible with the type is refused (400).

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text:
A key containing KEY, PASSWORD, TOKEN or SECRET is a secret: encrypted in the database (AES-256-GCM, ADR 0011), never returned by the API (********), never logged. It requires DOMINET_MASTER_KEY:

dominet gen-master-key          # prints a key: copy it into DOMINET_MASTER_KEY in the .env file

Back this key up separately from the database: without it, stored secrets are lost.

docs.title: Initial data
docs.text:
dominet seed [--dry-run]
  • Creates missing settings. Initial value: the environment variable of the same name if set (handy in Docker, e.g. SMS_FREE_KEY in .env), otherwise the default. Never overwrites an existing setting; safe to re-run.
  • Creates the default navigation (7 entries) only when the table is empty: an entry the administrator deleted or renamed is not recreated.
  • Checks everything before writing: on error (secret without master key, invalid value), nothing is written.
  • --dry-run shows what would be created without writing. Values are never printed.

docs.title: Routes (administrator)
docs.text:
Route Purpose GET /api/settings the 17 settings (display value, is_secret, is_set, from_default, readable) PUT /api/settings/{key} {"value": "..."} changes a setting; 400 if invalid, 404 if unknown, 503 for a secret without master key

Every change updates the cache immediately and notifies subscribed components (live reconfiguration).

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
637 Rust tests + 22 browser E2E scripts (604 checks). Everything runs locally: there is no automatic CI any more (ADR 0015, in French).

Command Contents Duration make ci formatting, clippy (server and WASM), Rust tests, cargo deny, cargo audit, sqlx metadata ≈ 2 min warm make e2e browser E2E on target/debug/dominet (after make front) ≈ 2.5 min make ci-full make ci + Docker image (build, smoke test) + E2E on the image depends on the Docker cache tools/stress-cold-render.sh [image] [n] [concurrency] [page] cold starts in a loop with concurrent requests: measures the Leptos stalled-render defect the guard works around (ADR 0021, in French); expected: 0 anomalies ≈ 3 s per start make hooks pre-push guard: make ci on a clean copy of the pushed commit

docs.title: Browser E2E (tools/e2e.sh)
docs.text:
Headless Firefox driven by Marionette (tests/e2e/marionette.py, no external Python dependency). The runner creates a throwaway database, a temporary Firefox profile and a server, replays the scripts, then deletes everything (even on failure):

Script Checks home.py server rendering, WASM hydration (menu collapse), live translations, session r2.py R2 journey through the UI only (no SQL): dashboard created from the invitation, one widget of tools/e2e.sh --image dominet:dev (or make e2e-image) replays everything on the Docker image: the only test that sees the production binary (built in release mode) together with its WASM files. A server and a WASM compiled differently give an inert interface (see PROJECT_CONTEXT.md, "Pièges connus"); only tests that really hydrate the page in a browser catch it.

docs.title: Adding a test
docs.text:
• A business rule → unit test in dominet-domain. A SQL query → repository test (dominet-store/tests).
  • A server function or a page → dominet/tests/ui.rs (always: anonymous, ordinary account, administrator).
  • Behaviour that only exists in the browser (hydration, click, WebSocket, CSP) → a script in tests/e2e/, added to the list in tools/e2e.sh. Forms are also tested without an input event (autofill).

docs.title: To improve — interface
docs.text: List kept by the user and by Claude; a ticked line is done.

docs.title: Page presentation (asked on 2026-11-07)
docs.text:
• [x] Line spacing and margins (CSS pass of 2026-11-08): card paragraphs, line height, vc-list lists. Still to be reviewed in the user's browser, page by page (dashboard, devices, energy, Android).
  • [x] Fields that overlap or misalign: generic crud forms on two columns (screen ≥ 960 px), checkboxes with their help text below, framed choice groups; messaging and Android forms moved to vc-form-group. /admin/cameras fields are grouped in pairs.
  • [x] "Write a message" page (/messaging/compose): stacked fields, channel and recipients in frames.
  • [x] Discovery page /surveillance/discovery: cards, one field per line (R6 lot 3).

Tool: SHOT_DIR=… tools/e2e.sh shots takes screenshots of several pages (list set with SHOT_PAGES, e.g. admin/cameras!add).

Proposed method: a single CSS pass (crates/dominet-web/style/main.css) then review in the user's browser, optimised build (RELEASE=1 make dev-run). One page at a time, before/after screenshots if useful.

docs.title: Other
docs.text: • The development WASM (48 MB) makes the interface slow to react: use RELEASE=1 make dev-run, or reduce the development WASM profile (opt-level, wasm-opt).

docs.title: Language follow-ups (English-first repository)
docs.text:
• Local assistant is French-only: its system prompt, the phrases it detects ("do you want me to continue?"), the action-card texts and the tool-result markers are in French on purpose (the assistant answers in French). Generalising it means translating them, answering in the user's language and replaying the evaluation set (make agent-eval).
  • MCP scope identifiers are French (lecture, pilotage; configuration and administration are shared): they are stored in token rows. Renaming them to read / control needs a data migration with accepted aliases.
  • Notification texts (alert e-mails and SMS, device messages) are English now; a per-account language is not implemented.
  • Code comments are mostly French (several thousand lines): they are translated gradually; new code is commented in English.
  • Example data in configuration schemas (names such as "Fermeture du soir") and the French aliases accepted for configuration kinds (regle_d_alerte…) stay as they help a French-speaking model.

docs.title: Licences follow-ups
docs.text:
• wg-easy: version 14 (pinned for the optional VPN) is reported as non-commercial (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0); version 15 is AGPL-3.0 but a rewrite. Verify at the source, then move to 15 (configuration, wgpw command in DEPLOY.md) and test the VPN profile. See Licences.
  • Open-Meteo attribution: show "Weather data by Open-Meteo.com" next to weather data in the interface (CC BY 4.0); today it is only in the documentation.
  • Re-read the pinned tags (reduct/store:v1.21.5 and the other images marked "known") before the first public release.
  • Camera viewing without a password on the LAN (RTSP 8554, WebRTC 8189): add per-viewer credentials in MediaMTX and in the application. See Security.
  • SECRET_KEY is read by the configuration but no code uses it: remove it, or use it.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Start with the diagnosis, it is read-only and says what to fix:

make prod-doctor

It checks the machine (configuration file, disk space, certificate), the services (running, restarting, unhealthy), the web address, then asks the application itself (database, migrations, administrator account, master key, MQTT, ReductStore). Each finding is OK, WARNING (works, but you should know) or BLOCKING (something does not work), with the command that fixes it. Its exit code is non-zero when something blocks. The application part alone is docker compose exec dominet dominet doctor.

docs.title: Common cases
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause What to do The installer stops with "port 443 is already used" Another web server on the machine Stop it, or move DomiNet's ports in .env (NGINX_HTTPS_PORT) The browser warns about the certificate The device does not know your local authority yet Open http://<address>/dominet-ca.crt once and install it https://<name>.local does not resolve No mDNS on the client or on the machine Install avahi-daemon on the machine, or use the IP address and set LAN_DOMAIN Camera passwords are refused DOMINET_MASTER_KEY is empty or was replaced Restore the original key from your copy; a new key cannot read old secrets The first start is very long The image is being built locally Normal on a small machine (15 to 40 minutes); published images avoid it A service restarts in a loop See its log make prod-logs S=<service> N=100 Zigbee2MQTT loops with network commissioning timed out; the installer warns that the dongle may already hold a network The dongle had a Zigbee network, but the Zigbee2MQTT folder is empty: it tries to create a new network docker stop dominet-zigbee2mqtt-1 first. If the dongle held paired devices, restore its original Zigbee2MQTT folder (database.db, coordinator_backup.json, configuration.yaml) into deploy/zigbee2mqtt. Otherwise unplug and replug the dongle (USB 2.0 port, extension cable) and make prod-up Grafana restarts and the log says invalid email address for SMTP from_address config (nginx and the application then wait for it) DEFAULT_FROM_EMAIL ends with an IP address (for example dominet@192.168.1.104) Set DEFAULT_FROM_EMAIL=dominet@dominet.local in .env, then make prod-up. make prod-doctor reports it password authentication failed for user "dominet" (the migrate service fails, nothing else starts); the installer says "a database volume from an earlier installation exists" The PostgreSQL volume was created by an earlier installation with another password; a new .env cannot open it Put the old .env back and run ./install.sh --reuse. To start from scratch (erases that data): make prod-down, then docker volume rm dominet_postgres-data No data from devices MQTT or Zigbee2MQTT make prod-doctor, then make prod-logs S=mosquitto N=50

docs.title: Asking for help
docs.text: Run make prod-report (read-only: services, resources, logs, automations, alerts, backups) and attach its output. It contains no password; read it before sharing anyway.

• Status: accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: DomiNet is a Rust application for home automation and video surveillance. This record fixes its overall shape and the adjustments decided after the eight feasibility spikes (ADR 0002, 0003, 0005 to 0010).

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• One dominet binary (Axum + Tokio) with sub-commands and roles (--only web|mqtt|scheduler|video|publishers|discovery); supervised tasks with restart and backoff; /healthz, /readyz, /metrics. Only the discovery role is deployed apart (host network, WS-Discovery multicast).
  • Cargo workspace of 10 crates (domain ← automation/surveillance/notify/integrations ← store/mqtt ← server; proto shared by server and WASM; web for Leptos). domain has no I/O and no framework.
  • Front end: Leptos 0.8 SSR + hydration (ADR 0007). Data: PostgreSQL (sqlx 0.9) for configuration, users, aggregates and recent state; ReductStore for video, snapshots, detections and raw IoT (ADR 0002). Bus: MQTT rumqttc (ADR 0005) + Axum WebSocket. Live view: WHEP through MediaMTX (ADR 0010).
  • User scripts: sandboxed Rhai, no direct side effects (ADR 0006). Vision: ffmpeg subprocess behind FrameSource (ADR 0003), YOLO through ort (ADR 0009), hand-written ONVIF (ADR 0008).
  • Authentication: ADR 0004.
  • Deployment: Docker Compose (the official route) and a release binary; main target x86_64 (Intel Core i5-6500 mini PC), arm64 on a best-effort basis. glibc image (Debian slim): ONNX Runtime has no musl binary. Binaries are published at the x86-64-v2 baseline (never target-cpu=native); the heavy computation (ONNX Runtime) picks its own AVX2 kernels at run time.
  • Observability: structured tracing, Prometheus /metrics, Grafana.

docs.title: Adjustments from the spikes
docs.text:
• Storage: ReductStore = raw archive and threshold queries; all charts come from PostgreSQL.
  • ort only has release candidates: the version is pinned exactly and a parity test is mandatory on every upgrade.
  • Leptos stays on 0.8 (0.9.0-rc1 came out on 2026-10-31; leptos-fluent requires < 0.9).
  • Docker: the dominet service gets /dev/dri and the render group (VAAPI); MediaMTX publishes its ICE port unshifted; ReductStore needs a non-empty token.
  • ONVIF: adding a camera by IP is mandatory (some cameras do not answer multicast); OpenIPC has no ONVIF.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: • Any departure from these choices goes through a new ADR that replaces this one.

docs.title: 0002 — IoT storage: ReductStore (raw) + PostgreSQL (aggregates)
docs.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-31
  • Spike verdict: go

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Raw IoT data goes to ReductStore (iot bucket); aggregates and recent state go to PostgreSQL. ReductStore is not a time-series database (no aggregation). A spike (reduct-rs 1.21.0 against server 1.21.5, on an Intel Core i5-6500) validated the label model, performance on 1 million records and FIFO retention.

docs.title: Model tested
docs.text: Bucket iot, one entry dev_{device_id}, one record per state change: body = JSON of the full state (about 100 bytes), labels = one per tracked numeric key (temperature, humidity, battery, linkquality), timestamp in µs. Data set: 100 devices × 10,000 points (1 point / 10 s).

docs.title: Measurements
docs.text:
Measure Result Ingestion, 1 M records with 4 labels, 8 parallel streams, batches of 50 595 s = 1,680 records/s Single write (write_record) 818 records/s (1.2 ms) Storage 232 bytes/record (227 MB on disk for 1 M) Last hour of a device (about 300 records, bodies read) 11 ms Full history of a device (10,000 records), headers only / bodies read 367 ms / 1.1 s temperature > 28 on one device (labels, 10,000 → 2,312) 99 ms temperature > 28 AND battery < 90 67 ms temperature > 29.5 over all 100 entries (1 M scanned → 100,394) 3.7 s Last value of a device (read_record without timestamp) 0.6 ms Hourly average over 24 h, computed client side (8,600 points) 0.93 s FIFO quota 10 MB, 30,000 writes of 1 KB size bounded to 10.4 MB, oldest evicted by blocks

Numeric comparisons ($gt, $lt, $and) work on labels stored as strings.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• iot bucket as above; one label per numeric key of tracked_keys. Single write per message (the real rate of about 50–100 msg/s is far below 818/s); optional batches, capped at 50 records (see pitfalls).
  • Roles: ReductStore = raw archive, forensics and threshold queries; PostgreSQL = everything that feeds charts and dashboards (recent state, device_state_log, energy aggregates). An hourly aggregate computed from ReductStore (about 1 s per day per device) is too slow for an interactive display.
  • Retention: FIFO quota per bucket, configurable (AppSetting), proposed default 5 GB for iot (about 21 M records, months at the real rate since only changes of tracked_keys are written). device_state_log (PostgreSQL): retention in days, configurable, proposed default 30 days; daily aggregates are kept without limit.
  • max_block_size is left at the default for iot; set to 1 MB for the small test buckets.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A multi-entry threshold query ("all probes > X") costs a few seconds at 1 M records: fine for investigation, not for a real-time page.
  • The FIFO quota evicts by blocks, so the size oscillates around the quota (about ±1 block); real disk space needs a margin.
  • Numeric keys absent from a message have no label: conditional queries ignore them.

docs.title: Pitfalls found
docs.text:
• Batch size: batch metadata travels in HTTP headers; beyond about 50–100 records the server answers RequestHeaderFieldsTooLarge (even without labels at 200). write_record_batch (v2) accepts records from several entries.
  • Asynchronous bucket deletion: right after a DELETE, writes fail with "Bucket is being deleted"; retry.
  • BucketInfo exposes no record count: get it by summing EntryInfo.record_count. Bucket is not Clone (share it through Arc).
  • A non-empty RS_API_TOKEN is mandatory in 1.21; the image has neither wget nor curl.
  • Not covered here: the video/snapshots/detections buckets (records of several MB, streamed reads).

docs.title: 0003 — Video decoding: ffmpeg subprocess behind FrameSource
docs.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-31
  • Spike verdict: go for ffmpeg (VAAPI when available, software otherwise); no-go for openh264 as the default

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Motion detection, YOLO and snapshots need decoded images. No mature 100 % Rust H.264 decoder exists (retina does not decode). Candidates: an ffmpeg subprocess (raw-frame pipe), ffmpeg-next (C binding, needs the libav*-dev headers, absent from the host, not evaluated), openh264 (Cisco, software). The spike plus an ffmpeg bench ran on an Intel Core i5-6500 (Skylake, HD Graphics 530), ffmpeg 7.1.5, VAAPI driver iHD 25.2.3, 30 s clips captured without re-encoding from real cameras (720p15, 360p15 sub-stream, two 1080p models).

docs.title: Measurements (CPU as % of one core, per stream, per second of video)
docs.text:
From a file, at full speed (no network):

Stream Software -threads 1, 5 fps → 640×640 RGB VAAPI decode only VAAPI + 5 fps + hwdownload + software scale 1080p camera A 7.6 % 1.2 % 3.5 % 720p15 camera 9.4 % 0.9 % 2.5 % 1080p12 camera B 5.8 % 1.1 % 3.5 % 360p sub-stream 4.2 % 0.7 % 1.2 %

Live (RTSP/TCP from the cameras), 4 simultaneous streams, 5 fps to 640×640: software -threads 1 = 87 % of a core (22 % of the machine); VAAPI + hwdownload + software scale = 32 % of a core (8 % of the machine). No failure. Latency of the first image with a cold-started ffmpeg: 2.1 to 4.3 s (waiting for the key frame). Software decoding of every frame, for reference: 1080p ≈ 5–9 % of a core in bursts.

openh264 (1 thread, frame by frame): 720p = 19 % of a core (about 2× software ffmpeg); failures on two camera families (183 errors out of 211 access units, "no parameter set"; ffmpeg decodes them without error) even after regrouping into access units. Cause not elucidated in the time available; extra integration cost: RTP depacketising (retina) and no hardware decoding.

In a non-root Docker container (debian:trixie-slim + ffmpeg + intel-media-va-driver), VAAPI decoding works with --device /dev/dri and the host's render group added to the user.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• A FrameSource trait; default implementation: one long-lived ffmpeg per camera, reading the MediaMTX re-stream (not the camera directly), writing fixed-size raw frames at N fps to stdout (-vf fps=N,scale=W:H,format=rgb24); the process is supervised (restart with backoff) and its frames are read in batches.
  • Opportunistic hardware acceleration: at start-up, probe ffmpeg -hwaccel vaapi … -f null; if it succeeds → -hwaccel vaapi -hwaccel_output_format vaapi then fps=N,hwdownload,format=nv12,scale=…; otherwise fall back to software -threads 1. On a Raspberry Pi 5 (no hardware H.264 decoding) the software fallback is what runs.
  • On-demand snapshots: do not start a cold ffmpeg (2–4 s); serve the latest frame of the already active FrameSource or, with no active stream, decode one key frame (-skip_frame nokey, about 2 % of a core).
  • Docker: the image ships ffmpeg and intel-media-va-driver; the production Compose adds devices: [/dev/dri:/dev/dri] and group_add: ["${RENDER_GID}"] (the host render group GID, read by make prod-init).
  • openh264 and ffmpeg-next remain possible later implementations of FrameSource, not chosen by default.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The cameras' CPU budget is small (about 8 % of the machine for 4 cameras with VAAPI, 22 % in software): the bottleneck will be YOLO, not decoding.
  • The real stream resolution sometimes differs from the ONVIF profile: one camera streams at 1280×720 while its profile announces 1920×1080; on another, /stream is the 800×448 sub-stream and /stream1 the 1080p; one camera emits only about 7 frames/s in the captured clip. Frame sizes must therefore be read from the stream (ffprobe/ffmpeg output), not deduced from ONVIF.
  • The fps= filter upstream of hwdownload limits the GPU→CPU copy cost; it is what makes the VAAPI chain worthwhile.

docs.title: Pitfalls found
docs.text:
• scale_vaapi fails on this host ("requested VAProfile is not supported": no video-processing VPP); the hwdownload + software scale chain works. Installing libigfxcmrt7 had no effect. Remaining lead, untested: intel-media-va-driver-non-free (Debian non-free component, replaces intel-media-va-driver), which ships the non-free Intel kernels. Not adopted: the current chain costs 32 % of a core for 4 cameras and the Docker image only uses the free driver.
  • A bench that throws stderr away can time a failing command: the first "VAAPI + scale" figures were wrong for that reason (corrected above).
  • A copy (-c copy) of a Thingino sub-stream to a transport stream needs -bsf:v h264_mp4toannexb or a Matroska container.

docs.title: 0004 — Authentication and sessions
docs.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-31

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Already decided with the owner: server-side sessions (tower-sessions, PostgreSQL storage), argon2id passwords, admin / user roles, accounts created with dominet createsuperuser. What remains is the implementation detail and a version mismatch discovered during the spikes.

docs.title: Version mismatch (checked on crates.io on 2026-10-31)
docs.text:
• tower-sessions 0.15.0 (February 2026); argon2 0.6.0; sqlx 0.9.0; axum 0.8.9.
  • The official PostgreSQL store tower-sessions-sqlx-store 0.15.0 (January 2025) depends on tower-sessions 0.14 and sqlx 0.8: incompatible with tower-sessions 0.15 + sqlx 0.9.
  • axum-login 0.18 follows the same branch; not adopted (the need is simple: an extractor and a role check).

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
1. Stay on tower-sessions 0.14 + sqlx 0.8 + the official store — pins sqlx back and complicates sqlx-cli.
  2. Write our own SessionStore (trait of tower-sessions-core 0.15) on sqlx 0.9 — about fifty lines, and we control the schema.
  3. A fully home-made session layer — reinvents signed cookies, id rotation, expiry.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Option 2: dominet-store::sessions implements SessionStore (table session(id, data jsonb, expiry_date, user_id), indexes on expiry_date and user_id). The user_id column lets us invalidate every session of an account (password change, deactivation).
  • Expired sessions are purged by a scheduler task (schedule_job), not by a dedicated thread.
  • Passwords: argon2 (argon2id), random salt, transparent rehash at login when the parameters change.
  • Cookie: HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax, identifier regenerated at login (anti-fixation), idle and absolute durations configurable (AppSetting).
  • Anti brute-force: progressive lockout per (account, IP) pair stored in the database (login_attempt), plus per-IP rate limiting at the Axum level; identical error messages for unknown account / wrong password, with a dummy hash to equalise response times.
  • CSRF: Origin/Host header check on every unsafe request, plus a token for forms; WebSockets require the session and check Origin.
  • Roles: admin (full management) and user (viewing and commands); checked by an Axum RequireRole extractor reused by the Leptos server functions. Android tokens remain a separate mechanism (one UUID per device).
  • CLI: dominet createsuperuser, dominet passwd.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The home-made store is tested against a real PostgreSQL: creation, expiry, deletion, per-user invalidation.
  • Watch tower-sessions upgrades; if the official store catches up with sqlx 0.9 we can go back to it.

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text:
• Hashing: argon2id m = 64 MiB, t = 3, p = 1, about 126 ms per hash on the target Core i5-6500 (release build). The OWASP minimum (19 MiB, 2 passes) costs only about 23 ms: too light for a personal server. At most 4 concurrent hashes (64 MiB each); the hash is transparently replaced at login when its parameters are old.
  • Lockout: per (account, IP) pair 5 failures, per account 20, per IP 30, window and duration of 15 minutes. The per-pair threshold alone would let an attacker change IP without limit; the per-account threshold stops them at 20 tries per quarter of an hour.
  • Home-made session store (PgSessionStore) on sqlx 0.9; tower-sessions-core 0.15 still uses #[async_trait]. The user_id column is derived from the user_id key of the data.
  • Pitfall found by a test: Session::flush() destroys the session but keeps its identifier in memory, reused at the next save: session fixation stayed possible. flush() must be followed by cycle_id() (see auth::session::open). The test login_rotates_the_session_id_against_fixation locks this behaviour.
  • Lifetime: idle time (SESSION_IDLE_MINUTES) is handled by the session layer; the absolute duration (SESSION_MAX_DAYS) is checked on every request from the login instant stored in the session.
  • Usage details: docs/authentication.md.

docs.title: 0005 — MQTT client: rumqttc
docs.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-31
  • Spike verdict: go

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The integration bus is MQTT (Zigbee2MQTT, Linky, SolarMax, weather). A reliable Rust client is needed for dominet-mqtt: automatic reconnection, QoS 1, +/# wildcards, throughput well above the real load (about 50 devices at 1 Hz, i.e. a few tens of msg/s). Spike: rumqttc 0.25.1, development Mosquitto 2.0, Intel Core i5-6500.

docs.title: Measurements
docs.text: Test Result Topic matching, 19 cases (zigbee2mqtt/#, +/availability, solarmax/+/+, $SYS, empty levels…) own implementation: 19/19; rumqttc::matches diverges on $SYS/# (harmless here) 50 devices × 1 Hz, QoS 1, 10 s 500/500, no loss 2,000 msg/s, QoS 1, 10 s 20,000/20,000, no loss Maximum burst QoS 1 (43,000 msg/s sent) 49,251/50,000 received (749 lost), 33,800 msg/s received Maximum burst QoS 0 (285,000 msg/s sent) 50,000/50,000 received Broker down 5 s during 100 msg/s QoS 1 (persistent sessions) 3,000 sent, 0 missing, 1 duplicate; reconnection 0.6 s after the broker returned; re-subscribe on every ConnAck

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• dominet-mqtt is built on rumqttc (QoS 1 by default, clean_session = false, stable client identifier).
  • Supervised event loop: on error, wait 250 ms then poll() again (automatic reconnection); re-subscribe on every ConnAck so as not to depend on the broker-side session.
  • topic_matches is implemented in dominet-mqtt with its case table as unit tests; rumqttc::matches is not used.
  • Handle QoS 1 duplicates: consumers (device state, history) must be idempotent (per-second deduplication is already planned for device_state_log).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• At a heavy burst (≫ 1,000 msg/s) the broker may drop QoS 1 messages (Mosquitto's per-client queue): irrelevant at the real rate, to watch in load tests.
  • Pitfalls noted: detect inactivity on received Publish packets, not on poll() (PingResp restarts a naive timeout); docker compose exec needs </dev/null inside a while read loop.

docs.title: 0006 — Automation scripts: sandboxed Rhai host
docs.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-31
  • Spike verdict: go

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Plugins and source-handling code run user code. In Rust, scripts go through an embedded Rhai engine. Requirements: an API publish/get_device/scene/log_value, variables topic/payload/device, limits (operations, depth, size, time) and a hostile script stopped without affecting the process. Spike: Rhai 1.27.0, features sync, serde, no_module.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• 18 checks, 0 failures: legitimate script (full API), unknown get_device → (), invalid topic refused.
  • Hostile scripts all stopped in under 45 ms, stable memory (max RSS 5.6 → 6.7 MB): infinite loops, infinite recursion, string/array/map growth, pad to 2·10⁹, eval, import, 5,000-level nesting (rejected at parsing), 100+ publish.
  • Time limit (on_progress) validated alone, operations unlimited: stop at 250 ms.
  • Panic of a host function: isolated by a thread, the process survives.
  • Performance: script compiled once (AST), about 1 µs per execution, about 850,000 executions/s (without the realistic JSON conversion cost, in the order of ten µs).

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Rhai host in dominet-automation, engine rebuilt per execution (cheap) with: Engine::new_raw + StandardPackage, set_max_operations(200_000), set_max_call_levels(24), set_max_expr_depths(48, 24), strings ≤ 16 KB, arrays ≤ 2,000, maps ≤ 500, disable_symbol("eval"), no_module (no import), wall-clock limit of 250 ms through on_progress. These values are tuning parameters (AppSetting), not frozen constants.
  • No direct side effect: publish, scene, log_value append Effects (at most 100 per run) that the engine applies afterwards; get_device reads a snapshot supplied by the host. publish topics are validated (no wildcard, ≤ 256 characters).
  • print goes to the automation execution log; debug is ignored.
  • Execution in spawn_blocking (or a dedicated thread): a panic in a host function becomes a logged execution error, not a process stop. ASTs are cached per automation (invalidated on edit).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The time limit only acts between two Rhai operations: a heavy native function would not be interrupted. Bounded sizes (arrays, strings) and the absence of blocking host functions avoid it; any future host function must be non-blocking and bounded.
  • Scripts written in another language do not port as is: rewrite them in Rhai.

docs.title: 0007 — Front end: Leptos SSR + hydration, WebSocket, Fluent i18n
docs.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-31
  • Spike verdict: go

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The front end is a single Axum binary that renders Leptos on the server then hydrates in WASM (no separate SPA). The spike validates, end to end: SSR, hydration, WebSocket real time, a dark theme (CSS variables), FR/EN i18n with Fluent. Stack: Leptos 0.8.23, leptos_axum 0.8, leptos-fluent 0.3.1, cargo-leptos 0.3.11, Axum 0.8.

docs.title: Results
docs.text: Browser end-to-end test (headless Firefox ESR, Marionette protocol): 16/16. - SSR: complete HTML on the server; Accept-Language picks the language; the lang cookie wins over the header. - Hydration: interactive counter after the WASM loads. - Real time: tokio::sync::broadcast hub → WebSocket; values and counter updated without reload; automatic reconnection on the WASM side (1 s retry, page "connected" again 3 s after the server restarts). - i18n: hot FR/EN switch, <html lang> synchronised, page title, Fluent plurals ([one]/*[other]), language kept across reloads (cookie → SSR). - Theme: dark by default, light through data-theme on <html> (CSS variables). - Build: incremental dev ≈ 7 s; cold release ≈ 2 min 50 (4 cores). Release WASM opt-level = "z" + LTO + wasm-opt: 448 KB (190 KB gzip), JS 17 KB, server binary 9.7 MB.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Leptos 0.8.x (0.8.23). 0.9.0-rc1 was published the same day and leptos-fluent 0.3.1 requires < 0.9: reassess when 0.9 final and leptos-fluent support are out.
  • cargo-leptos for the build; a single dominet-web crate with ssr/hydrate features, shared types (WebSocket messages) in dominet-proto.
  • i18n: leptos-fluent with locales/{en,fr}/main.ftl, lang cookie + Accept-Language on the server, customise: |b| b.set_use_isolating(false) mandatory.
  • WebSocket client: direct web-sys (about 40 lines) with reconnection; application heartbeat and session authentication added afterwards.
  • End-to-end tests: Marionette/Firefox with no dependency is enough; Playwright needs Node, absent from the host.

docs.title: Pitfalls found
docs.text:
• Fluent wraps variables in bidi marks U+2068/U+2069, visible in tests and copy-paste → disable them (see above).
  • leptos-fluent has no hydrate feature (only ssr, axum, actix…); <html lang> must not be written by hand in the shell (duplicate of leptos-fluent's synchronisation).
  • cargo leptos serve does not rebuild on change (cargo leptos watch does); the env key of [package.metadata.leptos] is ignored by cargo-leptos 0.3.11.
  • Not covered here: theme persistence (localStorage), widget drag-and-drop, cargo leptos in CI/Docker (dependency cache).

docs.title: 0008 — ONVIF: a minimal hand-written SOAP client
docs.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-31
  • Spike verdict: go (with the reservations below)

docs.title: Context
docs.text: No mature, suitable ONVIF crate exists. What is needed: WS-Discovery, identity/capabilities/profiles, RTSP URI, PTZ (ContinuousMove/Stop/GetStatus, presets), imaging (IrCutFilter). The spike (reqwest + roxmltree + sha1/base64 + socket2) ran against 4 real cameras.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Camera Firmware ONVIF Result 192.168.1.60 Jooan Q3R Thingino stable Device/Media/PTZ/Imaging all OK; real PTZ pan (0 → 46.4°); IR-cut Auto → ON → Auto 192.168.1.42 Jooan A2R Thingino stable same all OK; PTZ 0 → 46.0°; IR-cut OK 192.168.1.30 Xiaomi Thingino master Device/Media only profiles + RTSP OK; no PTZ or imaging (expected) 192.168.1.50 Ascam (Vatilon PB1) vendor firmware Device/Media/PTZ/Imaging all OK; IR-cut ON → OFF → ON; service addresses on :80/onvif/Media… 192.168.1.29 "NVT IPC" (IPC_NT98566, ONVIF 16.12) NVT firmware Device/Media/PTZ/Imaging on :8899 (/onvif/Media, /onvif/PTZ, /onvif/imaging) auth OK (admin); profiles 4096×2160 and 704×576; IR-cut AUTO; real PTZ confirmed by image comparison (the camera turns), but GetStatus always returns 0,0: no readable position; mechanical stops (a long ContinuousMove takes it to the end of travel); the camera's own web interface is unusable (plugin too old): everything goes through ONVIF/RTSP 192.168.1.38 OpenIPC OpenIPC no ONVIF the 401 comes from the web interface: control through the OpenIPC API (openipc night backend)
  • Authentication WS-Security UsernameToken, PasswordDigest (base64(sha1(nonce + created + password))) accepted by the three families; the camera clock is read first with GetSystemDateAndTime (no auth) to correct Created (measured offset: 0 s here).
  • Unicast latencies: 12–110 ms per call (Thingino ≈ 15–50 ms, Ascam ≈ 50–90 ms).
  • WS-Discovery: from the host, 4 devices found in 4 tries with 3 probes 1 s apart and 6 s of listening (a single probe / 4 s: 3 of 4 once). The Q3R never answers multicast despite a working unicast ONVIF → manual add by IP (add-manual) stays indispensable. An unlisted device (192.168.1.29, port 8899) also answered.
  • PTZ: speed is not proportional to x on Thingino (≈ 100°/s as soon as non-zero); the accuracy of a movement depends on the delay between ContinuousMove and Stop (≈ 20–100 ms of HTTP jitter) → ± 3° after a round trip. GetStatus returns the position in degrees on Thingino.
  • GetStreamUri of the .29 camera returns a URL that contains the user name and password in clear (rtsp://…/user=admin_password=…_channel=1_stream=0…). Never log or display this value; always mask it (password=***).
  • The ONVIF service port is not always 80 (here 8899, spotted by WS-Discovery through XAddrs): the service URL is a camera parameter, discovery fills it in.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• dominet-surveillance::onvif: a hand-written SOAP client (envelope written by hand, answers parsed with roxmltree, chosen over quick-xml for its read-only DOM), limited to the calls used: GetSystemDateAndTime, GetDeviceInformation, GetCapabilities, GetProfiles, GetStreamUri, PTZ (ContinuousMove, Stop, GetStatus, presets), imaging (Get/SetImagingSettings).
  • Always authenticate with WS-Security digest with clock correction; never display or log passwords.
  • An HTTP client without connection reuse (pool_max_idle_per_host(0)): Thingino's ONVIF server closes the connection after each answer; reuse causes connection closed before message completed on the next call.
  • Service addresses come from GetCapabilities, never deduced from the host (the Ascam uses /onvif/Media, Thingino /onvif/media_service).
  • Discovery: 3 probes 1 s apart, 6 s of listening, interface chosen by the default route; a discovery role in host network.
  • Contract tests: SOAP answers of these cameras captured (without secrets) in tests/fixtures/onvif/.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Smooth PTZ control goes through ContinuousMove followed by Stop when the key is released, not through time-calibrated movements.
  • Cameras without ONVIF (OpenIPC) need a dedicated backend (NightControl::openipc) and manual entry of parameters.
  • Not covered: ONVIF events, SetSystemDateAndTime, HTTP Digest authentication (useful for the goform backend).

docs.title: 0009 — Object detection: YOLOv8n through ort
docs.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-31
  • Spike verdict: go with reservations (ort has no stable release; Intel GPU not evaluated)

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Reproduce the reference detector: YOLOv8n ONNX (12.9 MB), input 640×640 NCHW float32 RGB/255, output [1,84,8400], score ≥ 0.10, NMS IoU 0.45 (class-agnostic). Spike: ort 2.0.0-rc.15, prebuilt ONNX Runtime 1.31.0; reference: onnxruntime 1.31.1 CPU. Machine: Intel Core i5-6500 (Skylake, 4 cores, AVX2).

docs.title: Measurements (median of 60 passes, 640×640 input image)
docs.text:
Intra-op threads ort inference (Rust) Reference inference Rust total (pre + inference + post) 1 105.6 ms 109.0 ms 112 ms 2 60.0 ms 62.4 ms 67 ms 4 42.8 ms 41.7 ms 50 ms
  • Rust pre-processing (direct bilinear resize + normalisation + NCHW) ≈ 4.5 ms; post-processing + NMS ≈ 2 ms.
  • Parity: 10/10 detections of the reference found again (same class, box IoU > 0.9, score gap < 0.02) on 5 images (COCO "bus" image: 4 people + bus + umbrella; 3 images from real cameras).
  • OpenVINO (trial through onnxruntime-openvino): CPU provider 38.6 ms against 41.7 ms (+ ≈ 8 %, negligible); GPU provider unusable here (Intel OpenCL runtime intel-opencl-icd absent) → CPU fallback. Not evaluated on the iGPU.
  • Test binary: 31 MB (ONNX Runtime statically linked), dynamic dependencies libstdc++, libgcc_s, libm, libc. Session creation ≈ 75 ms.
  • Prebuilt ONNX Runtime binaries for ort: x86_64-linux-gnu and aarch64-linux-gnu (CPU); no musl → glibc image (Debian slim).

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• dominet-surveillance::yolo: ort (CPU), pure-Rust pre/post-processing, same contract as the reference (score ≥ 0.10 before NMS, the user threshold yolo_min_confidence applied by the caller).
  • Exactly pinned version (=2.0.0-rc.15): ort only has release candidates (moving API). An upgrade is an explicit task with a rerun of the parity test. Features: std, ndarray, download-binaries, tls-rustls, copy-dylibs (the default tls-native would need OpenSSL, absent).
  • A pool of workers with 1 intra-op thread each, rather than a multi-thread session: it is the most efficient per core (0.112 core·s per inference against 0.20 at 4 threads). Throughput target: ≈ 9 inferences/s per dedicated core.
  • Budget: YOLO sampled at 1–2 frames/s per camera (not at the video rate); 4 to 5 cameras at 2 frames/s ≈ 1 core of YOLO + ≈ 8 % of the machine for VAAPI decoding (ADR 0003). The number of workers and the frequency become settings (AppSetting).
  • glibc Docker image, models/yolov8n.onnx copied into the image, path through YOLO_MODEL_PATH.
  • Regression test: the reference COCO image and its detections (no sensitive data) live in tests/fixtures/yolo/; the parity test compares with these frozen values.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Single-frame latency is fine for event detection, not for tracking at video rate: consistent with the use (alerts, DetectionEvent).
  • The potential gain of the iGPU (HD 530, 24 EU) is probably modest against an AVX2 CPU and competes with VAAPI. intel-opencl-icd does not exist in Debian 13: the trial would need Intel's repository. Abandoned unless a real capacity need appears.
  • arm64 (Raspberry Pi 5): a prebuilt ONNX Runtime binary exists, performance not measured.

docs.title: Pitfalls found
docs.text:
• ort pulls native-tls by default to download its binaries at build: without libssl-dev, use tls-rustls; the build needs network access to cdn.pyke.io (plan for CI and the Dockerfile, or pre-download with ORT_LIB_LOCATION).
  • SessionBuilder errors are not Send: do not propagate them as they are into anyhow (convert them to a string).

docs.title: 0010 — Camera live view: WHEP client in Rust/WASM towards MediaMTX
docs.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-31
  • Spike verdict: go (reservation lifted: a real 720p live view was validated in a real browser, see below)

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Live view goes through WebRTC/WHEP: MediaMTX re-exposes the cameras' RTSP streams, and the front end (WASM) negotiates the session. Spike: about 140 lines of web-sys (RTCPeerConnection + fetch + getStats) integrated in the Leptos page of the first spike; MediaMTX 1.21.3 in development; a real camera (Thingino, H.264 High, RTSP/TCP ingest on two paths: 720p and 360p).

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Server-side signalling: MediaMTX ingests the two camera paths (ready, H264 track) and answers 201 + H.264 SDP (packetization-mode=1) to a WHEP H.264 offer (tested by a direct POST) for both paths.
  • WASM client: full negotiation (offer, ICE gathering, POST, answer, ontrack → <video>) in 51 ms, 25 frames/s, 0 frames lost, average jitter buffer 11 ms, jitter 0.6 ms, RTT 0 ms (loopback). Measured on a VP8 test source published in MediaMTX.
  • End-to-end latency (VP8 test source encoding the wall-clock time in the image; measured in the browser through canvas, 120 samples): median 40 ms, p95 59 ms, min 19 ms, max 59 ms — generation + VP8 encoding + RTSP + MediaMTX + WebRTC + decoding + rendering, on loopback.
  • First frame: 1.5 s after the click, dominated by the wait for a key frame (1 s GOP of the test source).
  • Test limit: Debian's Firefox ESR (153) advertises no H.264 in its WebRTC offer (VP8, VP9, AV1 only); the media.peerconnection.video.h264_enabled and OpenH264 GMP preferences change nothing in headless mode. H.264 decoding of a real camera in a browser could therefore not be checked automatically; neither could the real-camera latency (camera encoder included).
  • Reproduced in a real browser (Debian Firefox ESR in a VNC session): "WHEP HTTP 400", MediaMTX log closed: codecs not supported by client. Cause: Debian's firefox-esr package disables OpenH264 by default (pref("media.gmp-gmpopenh264.enabled", false)), so the WebRTC offer does not propose H.264. It is not a defect of the WHEP client.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• dominet-web::whep takes over the spike module (recvonly offer, ICE gathering ≤ 2 s, POST application/sdp, DELETE of the resource on close); the WHEP URL is built from the settings MEDIAMTX_WEBRTC_SCHEME / MEDIAMTX_WEBRTC_DOMAIN, behind nginx /webrtc/ in production (same origin, no CORS).
  • getStats statistics (frames decoded/lost, fps, jitter buffer, RTT) are shown in the camera widget and used for automatic reconnection (no frame decoded for N s → new session).
  • No transcoding in MediaMTX: the browser must decode the camera's H.264. For browsers without WebRTC H.264, planned fallback: MJPEG/refreshed snapshots through FrameSource (ADR 0003).
  • To validate on a browser that decodes WebRTC H.264 (Chrome, Edge, Safari, Mozilla's Firefox; or Debian Firefox ESR with media.gmp-gmpopenh264.enabled = true and the plugin installed). A Debian Firefox ESR without the setting will always show the 400 error: plan an explicit message in the UI ("this browser does not decode H.264") rather than a silent failure.

docs.title: Consequences / pitfalls
docs.text:
• ICE port published identically: MediaMTX announces its internal port (8189) to the browser; Compose must publish 8189:8189 in UDP and TCP without shifting (an 18189:8189 breaks the connection), and webrtcAdditionalHosts must list the address the browser reaches (127.0.0.1 in development; the LAN and VPN domain/IP in production).
  • The display delay depends on the camera's GOP: MediaMTX cannot ask an RTSP source for a key frame. Measure on real cameras; prefer GOPs ≤ 2 s.
  • Camera credentials appear in no repository file: the spike's MediaMTX paths were created live through the API (/v3/config/paths/add), the production config generates them from the database (mediamtx_sync).
  • The web-sys API is verbose but stable; each Rtc* type needs its Cargo feature.

docs.title: 0011 — Encryption of sensitive values at rest
docs.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-01

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Application settings contain secrets (a Free Mobile API key today; camera passwords, tokens and SMTP credentials later). PostgreSQL is backed up (pg_dump) and can be copied: a clear-text value in a dump or backup is a leak.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
1. Clear-text values, the database being "private" — simple, but any dump, backup or read-only access exposes the secrets.
  2. Disk or PostgreSQL encryption (TDE) — does not protect against a logical dump or SQL access.
  3. Application-level encryption of sensitive values with a master key kept outside the database — chosen.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• AES-256-GCM (crate aes-gcm 0.11), a 32-byte master key in base64 in DOMINET_MASTER_KEY (the .env file, never in the database or in git). dominet gen-master-key generates one.
  • Stored format: v1: + base64( 96-bit nonce ‖ ciphertext ‖ tag ). The version prefix allows changing the algorithm later.
  • Associated data = the setting name: a ciphertext copied into another setting's row does not decrypt (tested).
  • Random nonce at every encryption: two ciphertexts of the same text differ.
  • Which settings: those whose key contains KEY, PASSWORD, TOKEN or SECRET, marked is_secret; the domain refuses to save a sensitive key not marked secret.
